result.markdown: --- title: "DATA100 Introduction to Data Analytics" subtitle: "Lecture 12: Data Tidying and Transformation Recap + Midterm Review" author: "Agassi Iu" institute: "Wilfrid Laurier University" date: "November 3, 2026" format: live-revealjs: theme: sky slide-number: true transition: slide incremental: true embed-resources: true # Embeds figures and libraries into a single portable HTML file filters: - live webr: packages: - dplyr - tidyr - tibble - stringr - forcats - lubridate execute: echo: true warning: false # Hides warnings and package loading messages message: false --- ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell autorun='true'} ```{webr} #| include: false #| autorun: true library(dplyr) library(tidyr) library(tibble) library(stringr) library(forcats) library(lubridate) ``` ::: # Midterm review ## What the midterm covers {.smaller} | Lecture | The problem we solved | Chapter | |-------------|-------------------|---------| | 8: Logical vectors | Do students who sleep less get lower grades? | 12 | | 9: Words and numbers | A sleep report: how much, when, and a readable chart | 13, 14, 16 | | 10: Fancy words and numbers | Finish cleaning `bedtime`, then find wake-up times | 15, 17 | | 11: Missing values and joins | Can we trust the survey? Does caffeine cost sleep? | 18, 19 | | 12: Pivoting (today) | Reading tables | 5 | ::: {.callout-note title="No survey data in this review"} Every example is small enough to work out **by hand**, like the midterm. If you can predict the output of a 3-row tibble, you can handle the big one. ::: ## How to use this review guide? 1. Ask yourself what does each line print? What is the anticipated output? 2. Click *Run Code* to see the output, and compare it with what you had in mind. 3. Try to explain your choices. If you were wrong, read the tip below and find out the reason of your mistake. ::: {.callout-tip title="What to look for on the midterm"} Almost every wrong answer comes from one of these: an `NA`, a recycled vector, a wrong order, or a key that does not match. Look for them first. ::: # Logical vectors ## Operators at a glance {.smaller} | Operator | Name | Returns | Example | Result | |----------|------|---------|---------|--------| | `&` | and | `TRUE` or `FALSE` | `TRUE & FALSE` | `FALSE` | | | | or | `TRUE` or `FALSE` | TRUE | FALSE | `TRUE` | | `!` | not | `TRUE` or `FALSE` | `!TRUE` | `FALSE` | | `==` | equal to | `TRUE` or `FALSE` | `5 == 5` | `TRUE` | | `%in%` | is in a list | `TRUE` or `FALSE` | `2 %in% c(1, 2, 3)` | `TRUE` | | `%/%` | integer division | a number | `7%/%3` | `2` | | `%%` | remainder | a number | `7 %% 3` | `1` | ::: {.callout-warning title="Watch out for"} - `==` tests for equality. A single `=` assigns a value - With an `NA`, most of these return `NA` (`NA %in% NA` is the exception) ::: ## Comparisons and `NA` {.smaller} What does each line print? ::: {.cell} ```{webr} x <- c(3, NA, 8, 5) x > 4 sum(x > 4) sum(x > 4, na.rm = TRUE) mean(x > 4, na.rm = TRUE) ``` ::: . . . ::: {.callout-note title="Tracing the code"} | Line | Result | Why | |-----|-----|---------| | `x > 4` | `FALSE`, `NA`, `TRUE`, `TRUE` | the `NA` stays `NA` | | `sum(x > 4)` | `NA` | one unknown makes the total unknown | | `sum(x > 4, na.rm = TRUE)` | 2 | counts the `TRUE`s among the known values | | `mean(x > 4, na.rm = TRUE)` | 0.667 | 2 out of **3** known values, not 2 out of 4 | ::: ## Boolean algebra with `NA` {.smaller} ::: {.cell} ```{webr} x <- c(TRUE, FALSE, NA) x & NA x | NA NA == NA NA %in% NA ``` ::: . . . ::: {.callout-note title="Truth table"} | `x` | `x & NA` | x | NA | |-----|----------|--------------------------| | `TRUE` | `NA` | `TRUE` | | `FALSE` | `FALSE` | `NA` | | `NA` | `NA` | `NA` | ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="One rule for all of them"} If the answer is the same whichever way the `NA` resolves, you get that answer (`FALSE & NA` is `FALSE`, `TRUE | NA` is `TRUE`). Otherwise you get `NA`. `NA == NA` is `NA`, but `NA %in% NA` is `TRUE` because `%in%` follows different rules. ::: ## Why `TRUE | FALSE` is `TRUE`, and `TRUE & FALSE` is `FALSE` {.smaller} ::: {.callout-note title="OR (`|`): at least one must be true"} - Example: "In order to pass this course, you must score 90% on the final exam **or** submit a 80-page final report for your group project." - Scenario: You score 91% on your final exam (`TRUE`) but you did not submit the final report (`FALSE`) - Did you pass? **Yes!** Because you fulfilled at least one of the passing requirements - So `TRUE | FALSE` is `TRUE`: a single `TRUE` satisfies the rule - That's why `TRUE|NA` is also `TRUE` since both `TRUE|TRUE` and `TRUE|FALSE` give `TRUE ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="AND (`&`): both must be true"} - Example: "In order to pass this course, you must score 90% on the final exam **and** submit a 80-page final report for your group project." - Scenario: You score 91% on your final exam (`TRUE`) but you did not submit the final report (`FALSE`) - Did you pass? **No!** The condition requires you to both score above 90% on the exam and submit the final report! You only did half the work - So `TRUE & FALSE` is `FALSE`: one `FALSE` breaks the rule - That's why `FALSE&NA` is also `FALSE` since both `FALSE&TRUE` and `FALSE&FALSE` give `FALSE ::: ## The `filter()` traps {.smaller} `pull(stress)` shows which values survive the filter. ::: {.cell} ```{webr} df <- tibble(stress = c(1, 4, 5, 2, NA)) df |> filter(stress == 4 | 5) |> pull(stress) df |> filter(stress %in% c(4, 5)) |> pull(stress) df |> filter(stress == NA) |> pull(stress) df |> filter(is.na(stress)) |> pull(stress) ``` ::: . . . ::: {.callout-note title="Tracing the code"} | Filter | Rows kept | What happened? | |------|------|------------| | stress == 4 | 5 | **all 5**, even the `NA` | `5` counts as `TRUE`, and `NA | TRUE` is `TRUE` | | `stress %in% c(4, 5)` | 4 and 5 | `%in%` never returns `NA` | | `stress == NA` | none | `== NA` is always `NA`, and `filter()` drops `NA` | | `is.na(stress)` | the `NA` row | the right way to find blanks | ::: ## `case_when()` {.smaller} ::: {.cell} ```{webr} hours <- c(5, 7, 9, NA) case_when(hours < 6 ~ "Short", hours <= 7.5 ~ "Normal", hours > 7.5 ~ "Long") case_when(hours <= 7.5 ~ "Normal", hours < 6 ~ "Short", hours > 7.5 ~ "Long") case_when(hours < 6 ~ "Short", hours <= 7.5 ~ "Normal", .default = "Long") ``` ::: . . . ::: {.callout-note title="Tracing the code"} | `hours` | Line 1 | Line 2 (Normal first) | Line 3 (`.default`) | |---------|--------|-----------------------|---------------------| | 5 | Short | **Normal** | Short | | 7 | Normal | Normal | Normal | | 9 | Long | Long | Long | | `NA` | `NA` | `NA` | **Long** | ::: ::: {.callout-warning title="Watch out for"} - Only the **first** `TRUE` condition is used, so order matters (line 2 never says `"Short"`) - `.default` also catches the `NA` (anything that does not satisfies the previous conditions get lumped into the `.default` category) ::: # Words and numbers ## Recycling {.smaller} ::: {.cell} ```{webr} x <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6) x * c(1, 2) x * c(1, 2, 3, 4) program <- c("Business", "Arts", "Arts", "Business") program == c("Arts", "Business") program %in% c("Arts", "Business") ``` ::: . . . ::: {.callout-note title="Compare position by position"} | `program` | recycled partner | `==` | `%in%` | |-----------|------------------|------|--------| | Business | Arts | `FALSE` | `TRUE` | | Arts | Business | `FALSE` | `TRUE` | | Arts | Arts | `TRUE` | `TRUE` | | Business | Business | `TRUE` | `TRUE` | ::: ::: {.callout-warning title="Watch out for"} - `==` does not ask "is this one of the two?". That is the job of `%in%` - Lengths 6 and 2 recycle silently. Lengths 6 and 4 still compute, but R warns that 6 is not a multiple of 4 ::: ## `pmin()`, ranks, and the mean {.smaller} ::: {.cell} ```{webr} a <- c(1, 5, 7) b <- c(3, 2, NA) pmin(a, b, na.rm = TRUE) min(a, b, na.rm = TRUE) min_rank(c(30, 10, 20, 10)) min_rank(desc(c(30, 10, 20, 10))) mean(c(0, 0, 0, 1, 20)) median(c(0, 0, 0, 1, 20)) ``` ::: . . . ::: {.callout-note title="Tracing the code"} | Line | Result | What happened? | |------|---|----------| | `pmin(a, b, na.rm = TRUE)` | 1, 2, 7 | row by row; the `NA` is ignored, so row 3 is 7 | | `min(a, b, na.rm = TRUE)` | 1 | one value for everything | | `min_rank(c(30, 10, 20, 10))` | 4, 1, 3, 1 | the two 10s share rank 1, so the next rank is 3 | | `min_rank(desc(...))` | 1, 3, 2, 3 | `desc()` flips the order | | `mean()` and `median()` | 4.2 and 0 | one large value pulls the mean up | ::: ## `%/%`, `%%`, `round()` and `cut()` {.smaller} ::: {.cell} ```{webr} 25 %/% 7 25 %% 7 round(123.456, 1) round(123.456, -1) x <- c(0, 5, 6, 10) cut(x, breaks = c(0, 5, 10), labels = c("low", "high")) cut(x, breaks = c(0, 5, 10), labels = c("low", "high"), right = FALSE) ``` ::: . . . ::: {.callout-note title="Which bin?"} | `x` | Default: `(0, 5]`, `(5, 10]` | `right = FALSE`: `[0, 5)`, `[5, 10)` | |-----------|---------------------------|-----------------------------------| | 0 | `NA` | low | | 5 | low | high | | 6 | high | high | | 10 | high | `NA` | ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="Tip"} - A negative `digits` rounds to the left of the decimal point: `-1` is the nearest ten - Values outside the breaks become `NA` ::: ## Strings and `NA` {.smaller} ::: {.cell} ```{webr} name <- c("Flora", NA, "Terra") str_c("Hi ", name, "!") str_length(c("a", "R for data", NA)) str_to_lower(str_trim(" PM ")) ``` ::: . . . ::: {.callout-note title="Tracing the code"} | Line | Result | Why | |-------|----|--------| | `str_c("Hi ", name, "!")` | `"Hi Flora!"`, `NA`, `"Hi Terra!"` | an `NA` input gives an `NA` output | | `str_length(c("a", "R for data", NA))` | 1, 10, `NA` | spaces count as characters | | `str_to_lower(str_trim(" PM "))` | `"pm"` | trim the spaces, then lower the capitals | ::: ## Splitting text {.smaller} The first attempt fails. What does the fixed attempt give? ::: {.cell} ```{webr} #| error: true times <- tibble(bedtime = c("11:30 pm", "midnight", "around 11 pm")) times |> separate_wider_delim(bedtime, delim = " ", names = c("time", "ampm")) times |> separate_wider_delim( bedtime, delim = " ", names = c("time", "ampm"), too_few = "align_start", too_many = "merge" ) ``` ::: . . . ::: {.callout-note title="Why the first attempt errors"} | `bedtime` | Pieces | Problem | |-----------|--------|---------| | 11:30 pm | 2 | fits | | midnight | 1 | too few | | around 11 pm | 3 | too many | ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="The fixed attempt"} | time | ampm | |------|------| | 11:30 | pm | | midnight | `NA` | | around | 11 pm | ::: ::: {.callout-warning title="Watch out for"} `align_start` fills the missing piece with `NA`, and `merge` glues the extra pieces onto the last column. The last row is still wrong (`around` is not a time), so tidy the text first. ::: ## Factors {.smaller} ::: {.cell} ```{webr} month_levels <- c("Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr") f <- factor(c("Mar", "Jan", "Jam", "Apr"), levels = month_levels) f sort(f) n <- tibble(drink = c("Coffee", "Tea", "Pop"), n = c(30, 50, 10)) levels(fct_reorder(n$drink, n$n)) fct_collapse(n$drink, Hot = c("Coffee", "Tea")) ``` ::: . . . ::: {.callout-note title="Tracing the code"} | Line | Result | What happened? | |------|-----|--------| | `f` | Mar, Jan, `NA`, Apr | `"Jam"` is not in `levels`, so it is silently `NA` | | `sort(f)` | Jan, Mar, Apr | sorted by the level order, and the `NA` is dropped | | `levels(fct_reorder(drink, n))` | Pop, Coffee, Tea | levels sorted by `n`, smallest first | | `fct_collapse(drink, Hot = ...)` | Hot, Hot, Pop | levels you do not mention (Pop) stay the same | ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="Tip"} Smallest first is why the biggest bar ends up at the top of a sideways chart. ::: # Lecture 10: Fancy words and numbers ## Does it match? {.smaller} ::: {.cell} ```{webr} x <- c("11:30 pm", "23:30", "midnight", "idk", "11:30 PM") str_detect(x, "pm") str_detect(x, regex("pm", ignore_case = TRUE)) str_detect(x, "\\d") str_detect(x, "^\\d{1,2}:\\d{2} ?(am|pm)$") ``` ::: . . . ::: {.callout-note title="Tracing the code"} | `x` | `"pm"` | `ignore_case` | `"\\d"` | Our desired format of time | |-----|--------|---------------|---------|------------| | 11:30 pm | `TRUE` | `TRUE` | `TRUE` | `TRUE` | | 23:30 | `FALSE` | `FALSE` | `TRUE` | `FALSE` | | midnight | `FALSE` | `FALSE` | `FALSE` | `FALSE` | | idk | `FALSE` | `FALSE` | `FALSE` | `FALSE` | | 11:30 PM | `FALSE` | `TRUE` | `TRUE` | `FALSE` | ::: ## Cleaning with a chain {.smaller} ::: {.cell} ```{webr} x <- c(" Around 11:30PM", "11.30 p.m.", "midnight") x |> str_trim() |> str_to_lower() |> str_remove("^(around|about|~) ?") |> str_replace("midnight", "12:00 am") |> str_replace("p\\.m\\.", "pm") |> str_replace("([0-9])(am|pm)", "\\1 \\2") |> str_replace("\\.", ":") ``` ::: . . . ::: {.callout-note title="Follow each string down the chain"} | After | `" Around 11:30PM"` | `"11.30 p.m."` | `"midnight"` | |-------------------------------|---------|---------|---------| | `str_trim()` and `str_to_lower()` | `"around 11:30pm"` | `"11.30 p.m."` | `"midnight"` | | `str_remove()` | `"11:30pm"` | `"11.30 p.m."` | `"midnight"` | | `str_replace("midnight", ...)` | `"11:30pm"` | `"11.30 p.m."` | `"12:00 am"` | | `str_replace("p\\.m\\.", ...)` | `"11:30pm"` | `"11.30 pm"` | `"12:00 am"` | | `str_replace("([0-9](am|pm)", ...)` | `"11:30 pm"` | `"11.30 pm"` | `"12:00 am"` | | `str_replace("\\.", ":")` | `"11:30 pm"` | `"11:30 pm"` | `"12:00 am"` | ::: ## Pulling pieces out, and the 24-hour rule {.smaller} ::: {.cell} ```{webr} tibble(clean = c("11:30 pm", "2330", "idk")) |> separate_wider_regex( clean, patterns = c(hh = "\\d{1,2}", ":?", mm = "\\d{0,2}", " ?", ampm = "am|pm|"), too_few = "align_start" ) df <- tibble(hh = c(11, 11, 23, 1, 12), ampm = c("pm", "", "", "", "")) df |> mutate( hour24 = case_when( ampm == "am" ~ hh %% 12, ampm == "pm" ~ hh %% 12 + 12, hh >= 13 | hh == 0 ~ hh, hh >= 6 & hh <= 11 ~ hh + 12, hh <= 5 | hh == 12 ~ hh %% 12 ) ) |> pull(hour24) ``` ::: . . . ::: {.callout-note title="The pieces"} | hh | mm | ampm | |----|----|------| | 11 | 30 | pm | | 23 | 30 | (empty) | | `NA` | `NA` | `NA` | ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="The 24-hour rule"} | hh | ampm | Applying the rule | `hour24` | |------|--------|-----------------|--------| | 11 | pm | `pm`: 11 %% 12 + 12 | 23 | | 11 | (empty) | 6 to 11, no `am` or `pm`: evening, add 12 | 23 | | 23 | (empty) | 13 or more: already 24-hour | 23 | | 1 | (empty) | 5 or less: after midnight | 1 | | 12 | (empty) | 12 with no `am` or `pm`: 12 %% 12 | 0 | ::: ## Creating date-times {.smaller} ::: {.cell} ```{webr} ymd("2026-10-27") mdy("October 27, 2026") dmy("27-Oct-2026") t <- ymd_hms("2026-10-27 06:35:00") hour(t) minute(t) day(t) wday(t, label = TRUE) make_datetime(2026, 10, 27) + hours(25) + minutes(30) ``` ::: . . . ::: {.callout-note title="Tracing the code"} | Line | Result | What happened? | |------|--------|---------------| | `ymd()`, `mdy()`, `dmy()` | everything returns to `2026-10-27` | the function name spells the order of the pieces | | `hour(t)`, `minute(t)` | 6 and 35 | returns hour and minute | | `day(t)`, `wday(t, label = TRUE)` | 27 and Tue | day of the month vs day of the week | | `make_datetime(...) + hours(25) + minutes(30)` | `2026-10-28 01:30:00 UTC` | 25 hours after midnight rolls over to 1 AM | ::: ::: {.callout-warning title="Watch out for"} With no `tz`, the time zone is UTC. ::: ## Periods, durations, and `%within%` {.smaller} ::: {.cell} ```{webr} start <- ymd_hms("2026-11-01 00:00:00", tz = "America/Toronto") start + days(1) start + ddays(1) bed <- ymd_hms("2026-10-27 23:30:00", tz = "America/Toronto") wake <- bed + dhours(7.5) check <- ymd_hms("2026-10-28 06:45:00", tz = "America/Toronto") wake check %within% interval(bed, wake) ``` ::: . . . ::: {.callout-note title="Tracing the code"} | Line | Result | Why | |---------|------|----------| | `start + days(1)` | `2026-11-02 EST` | a period moves the clock by one calendar day | | `start + ddays(1)` | `2026-11-01 23:00:00 EST` | a duration is exactly 24 hours, and that day has 25 | | `wake` | `2026-10-28 07:00:00 EDT` | 11:30 PM plus 7.5 hours | | `check %within% interval(bed, wake)` | `TRUE` | 6:45 AM is inside 11:30 PM to 7:00 AM | ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="Tip"} Sleep lasts a fixed amount of time, so we add it with `dhours()`. ::: # Missing values and joins ## Explicit and implicit missing {.smaller} Day 2 is explicit. Day 3 is implicit. What does `complete()` do? ::: {.cell} ```{webr} responses <- tibble(day = c(1, 2, 4), n = c(10, NA, 7)) mean(responses$n) mean(responses$n, na.rm = TRUE) responses |> complete(day = 1:4, fill = list(n = 0)) ``` ::: . . . ::: {.callout-note title="The table after `complete()`"} | day | n | Was it missing? | |-----|---|------| | 1 | 10 | present | | 2 | `NA` | explicit missing | | 3 | 0 | implicit missing | | 4 | 7 | present | ::: ::: {.callout-warning title="Watch out for"} `fill` only applies to rows `complete()` adds, so the explicit `NA` on day 2 stays. To fix that one too, add `mutate(n = replace_na(n, 0))`. ::: ## The `NA` counting trap {.smaller} ::: {.cell} ```{webr} sleep <- c(5, NA, 7, 8, NA, 4) sum(sleep < 6) sum(sleep < 6, na.rm = TRUE) sum(sleep >= 6, na.rm = TRUE) sum(is.na(sleep)) tibble(sleep) |> filter(sleep < 6) |> nrow() ``` ::: . . . ::: {.callout-note title="Where the 6 students went"} | Group | Count | Values | |-------|-------|--------| | `sleep < 6` | 2 | 5, 4 | | `sleep >= 6` | 2 | 7, 8 | | `NA` | 2 | in neither group | | Total | 6 | | ::: ## Handling `NA` {.smaller} ::: {.cell} ```{webr} x <- c(10, NA, 30, NA) replace_na(x, 0) coalesce(x, 99) na_if(c(72, -99, 85), -99) filled <- replace_na(x, mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)) c(mean(x, na.rm = TRUE), mean(filled)) c(sd(x, na.rm = TRUE), sd(filled)) ``` ::: . . . ::: {.callout-note title="Tracing the code"} | Line | Result | What happened? | |------|--------|-----| | `replace_na(x, 0)` | 10, 0, 30, 0 | every `NA` becomes 0 | | `coalesce(x, 99)` | 10, 99, 30, 99 | the first value that is not `NA` | | `na_if(c(72, -99, 85), -99)` | 72, `NA`, 85 | the code `-99` becomes a real `NA` | | mean before and after filling | 20 and 20 | the mean of the known values does not move | | `sd` before and after filling | 14.14 and 8.16 | the filled values sit at the mean, so the spread shrinks | ::: ## Join types {.smaller} ::: {.cell} ```{webr} x <- tibble(key = c(1, 2, 3), x_value = c("a", "b", "c")) y <- tibble(key = c(1, 2, 4), y_value = c("A", "B", "D")) inner_join(x, y, by = "key") left_join(x, y, by = "key") full_join(x, y, by = "key") anti_join(x, y, by = "key") semi_join(x, y, by = "key") ``` ::: . . . ::: {.callout-note title="Tracing the code"} | Join | Rows | Keys | Columns | |------|------|------|---------| | `inner_join()` | 2 | 1, 2 | both | | `left_join()` | 3 | 1, 2, 3 | both, `y_value` is `NA` for key 3 | | `full_join()` | 4 | 1, 2, 3, 4 | both, `NA` on either side | | `anti_join()` | 1 | 3 | `x` only | | `semi_join()` | 2 | 1, 2 | `x` only | ::: ## A key that does not match {.smaller} ::: {.cell} ```{webr} students <- tibble(id = 1:3, favourite_drink = c("Coffee", "coffee", "Tea")) drinks <- tibble(drink = c("Coffee", "Tea"), caffeine_mg = c(95, 47)) drinks |> count(drink) |> filter(n > 1) students |> left_join(drinks, by = join_by(favourite_drink == drink)) students |> anti_join(drinks, by = join_by(favourite_drink == drink)) ``` ::: . . . ::: {.callout-note title="The `left_join()` result"} | id | favourite_drink | caffeine_mg | |----|-----------------|-------------| | 1 | Coffee | 95 | | 2 | coffee | `NA` | | 3 | Tea | 47 | ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="Tip"} - Line 4 gives 0 rows: no `drink` appears twice, so `drink` is a **primary key** of `drinks` - Line 7 returns exactly student 2: `anti_join()` finds the rows with no match - `favourite_drink` is the **foreign key**: it holds values that should exist in the primary key of the other table ::: ::: {.callout-warning title="What to watch out for"} No error. One lowercase letter and the join silently gives `NA`. ::: # Pivoting ## Why pivot? {.smaller} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Wide**: one column per quiz | student | quiz1 | quiz2 | quiz3 | |---------|-------|-------|-------| | Jerry | 80 | 90 | 85 | | Ben | 70 | 75 | `NA` | ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Long**: one row per student and quiz | student | quiz | score | |---------|------|-------| | Jerry | quiz1 | 80 | | Jerry | quiz2 | 90 | | Jerry | quiz3 | 85 | | Ben | quiz1 | 70 | | Ben | quiz2 | 75 | | Ben | quiz3 | `NA` | ::: :::: - The wide table is easy for people to read - Most *R* tools want the long one: `ggplot2` maps `quiz` to the x-axis or a colour, and `group_by(quiz)` needs a `quiz` column - Pivoting changes the **shape**, not the information ## Same data, two shapes {.smaller} ::: {.callout-note title="Tidy data: three rules"} 1. Each variable is a column 2. Each observation is a row 3. Each value is a cell The wide table breaks rule 1: `quiz` is one variable, but its values are spread across three column names. ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="Coming from Excel?"} An Excel *pivot table* is roughly `count()` followed by `pivot_wider()`. The book calls the tools `pivot_longer()` and `pivot_wider()`. ::: ## A tiny example {.smaller} ::: {.cell} ```{webr} x <- tibble( student = c("Jerry", "Ben"), quiz1 = c(80, 70), quiz2 = c(90, 75), quiz3 = c(85, NA) ) x long <- x |> pivot_longer(cols = quiz1:quiz3, names_to = "quiz", values_to = "score") long long |> pivot_wider(names_from = quiz, values_from = score) ``` ::: . . . ::: {.callout-note title="What happened"} - `pivot_longer()`: 2 rows and 4 columns became 6 rows and 3 columns. The old column names (`quiz1`, `quiz2`, `quiz3`) went into `quiz`, and the old values went into `score` - `pivot_wider()`: the last call gives back exactly `x` ::: ## `pivot_longer()`: definition {.smaller} ::: {.callout-note title="`pivot_longer()`"} This function makes a table **longer**: it takes several columns and stacks them into rows. You get fewer columns and more rows. Use it when the column names are really values (`quiz1`, `quiz2`, `wk1`, `2024`). ::: ```r data |> pivot_longer( cols = quiz1:quiz3, # which columns to stack names_to = "quiz", # new column for the old column NAMES values_to = "score" # new column for the old column VALUES ) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Three questions to ask when you construct this table"} 1. Which columns hold values? (e.g. `quiz1:quiz3`, `-student`, `starts_with("quiz")`, `everything()`) 2. What do I call the column for the names? 3. What do I call the column for the values? ::: ## `pivot_longer()`: examples {.smaller} ::: {.cell} ```{webr} x <- tibble( student = c("Jerry", "Ben"), quiz1 = c(80, 70), quiz2 = c(90, 75), quiz3 = c(85, NA) ) # Everything except student x |> pivot_longer(-student, names_to = "quiz", values_to = "score") # Drop the missing score x |> pivot_longer(-student, names_to = "quiz", values_to = "score", values_drop_na = TRUE) # Clean the names: "quiz1" becomes the number 1 x |> pivot_longer(-student, names_to = "quiz", values_to = "score", names_prefix = "quiz", names_transform = as.integer) # From Lecture 11: counting the NAs in every column mini <- tibble(sleep = c(7, NA, 6), stress = c(NA, NA, 4)) mini |> summarize(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))) |> pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "column", values_to = "missing") ``` ::: . . . ::: {.callout-note title="What each option does"} | Option | Effect | |-----|___--------| | `values_drop_na = TRUE` | removes the rows where the value is `NA` (5 rows instead of 6) | | `names_prefix = "quiz"` | removes `"quiz"` from the front of each name | | `names_transform = as.integer` | turns the names from text into numbers | | last example | one row per column: `sleep` has 1 missing, `stress` has 2 | ::: ## `pivot_wider()`: definition {.smaller} ::: {.callout-note title="`pivot_wider()`"} This function makes a table **wider**: it spreads the values of one column into several new columns. You get more columns and fewer rows. Use it when you want a grid that people can read, or to put two groups side by side. ::: ```r data |> pivot_wider( names_from = quiz, # column whose VALUES become the new column names values_from = score, # column whose values fill the new cells values_fill = 0 # optional: what to put in an empty cell ) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="How rows are merged"} All the other columns identify the row. Rows with the same values in those columns are merged into one row. ::: ## `pivot_wider()`: examples {.smaller} ::: {.cell} ```{webr} orders <- tibble( day = c("Mon", "Mon", "Tue", "Tue"), item = c("tea", "coffee", "tea", "tea") ) orders |> count(day, item) orders |> count(day, item) |> pivot_wider(names_from = item, values_from = n) orders |> count(day, item) |> pivot_wider(names_from = item, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) ``` ::: . . . ::: {.callout-note title="Another way to express the table"} | day | coffee | tea | |-----|--------|-----| | Mon | 1 | 1 | | Tue | `NA` (or 0 with `values_fill`) | 2 | ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="Link to Lecture 11"} On Tuesday nobody ordered coffee, so `count()` has **no row** for it: implicit missing. `pivot_wider()` turns it into an explicit `NA`, and `values_fill = 0` replaces it, like `complete()` did. ::: ::: {.callout-warning title="Watch out for"} `"tea"` and `"Tea"` are different values, so they become **two** columns. ::: ## Which one should I use? {.smaller} | You have... | Use | Because | |--------------|-----|--------| | column names that are really values (`quiz1`, `wk1`, years) | `pivot_longer()` | each value belongs in a cell of one column | | a plot to draw (colour, facets, an axis) | `pivot_longer()` | `ggplot2` needs one column for each of these | | a `group_by()` and `summarize()` across those columns | `pivot_longer()` | you can only group by a column | | counts from `across()` (Lecture 11) | `pivot_longer()` | one row per column, ready to plot | | a column of categories and a number, and you want a grid to read | `pivot_wider()` | a compact table for a report | | two groups side by side and you want to subtract them (`quiz2 - quiz1`) | `pivot_wider()` | arithmetic across columns is easy | # Announcements ## Next Class ::: {.callout-important title="Midterm practice!"} You should probably come to next class as we don't have any practice problems for the upcoming midterm. ::: ::: {.callout-caution title="Group project"} You should have found a group of 4-5 for the final project by now. if you don't have a group, please let me know so that I can put you in a group (randomly). ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="Studying tips for the midterm"} Review your lab assignments (both pre and in-lab). <script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
